name: Nüzhen 女真
confidence_why: Jurchen is extinct and known only through Chinese-character and Jurchen-script transcriptions; Jin Guangping & Jin Qizong (1980) state that it had no tonal distinctions and that the middle syllable of trisyllabic words was pronounced weakly or dropped, but neither they nor Grube (1896), Kane (1975, 1989), Daoerji & Hexige (1983), Pevnov (1992, 1997) or Joseph (2018) say where word stress fell, so its placement is left undetermined.

catalog_locator: Ch.5 女真文字的讀音 (pp.108-183): sec.2 p.131 and sec.3 p.157 on the irrelevance of the four Chinese tones; sec.3 p.162 and sec.5 pp.178-179 on the weak/syncopated medial syllable of trisyllables.

new_statements.translation: p.157: These transcription characters all differ from one another, and their four tones also differ, but this cannot be counted as two or three readings. Because Jurchen characters have no four-tone distinction, although the transcribing Chinese characters differ, the sound of the character has in fact not changed. | p.131: As for the four tones ping, shang, qu, ru, they bear no relation whatsoever in the Jurchen language. | p.178: In addition, the middle syllable of trisyllabic words also often uses u in yang-class words; this is because in Jurchen trisyllabic words the middle syllable is usually read light [weak], even approaching a medial consonant, e.g. nomuxo = momxo, dʒomuʃin = dʒomʃin, boluwun = bol(x)un, dʒaluxa = dʒalxa, dabusun = dabsun, tao'unra = taonra. | p.162: Here it is read simply as 'r/l', probably because it is the middle syllable of a polysyllabic word and rapid pronunciation reads 'lu' as 'l'.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no Jurchen record and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to agree with or contradict. This work supplies the first prosodic facts on record for Jurchen: (1) non-tonal per the source; (2) medial syllable of trisyllables weak/syncopating. It gives no stress placement. Reading tagged 'unclear' because a statement exists but does not settle the type; it is not internally contradictory.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement of primary word stress is stated anywhere in the book; there is no stress/accent (重音) section. The book states that Jurchen is not tonal (the Chinese tones of the transcription characters are irrelevant; 'Jurchen characters have no four-tone distinction') and that the middle syllable of trisyllabic words is habitually read weak (輕讀), reducing to a consonant or syncopating (dabusun > dabsun). That is compatible with prominence on a non-medial syllable (initial or final) but the source does not say which, so no placement type can be assigned.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Only the medial-syllable reduction statement (pp.178-179, 162) bears on rhythm.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. Vowel harmony exceptions and loanword non-harmony are discussed (p.179) but not prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: The book describes Jin-dynasty (12th-13th c.) Jurchen as recorded in the Jurchen-script inscriptions, corrected against the Ming-period Hua-Yi yiyu 'Nüzhen yiyu' vocabularies (Yongle and Huitongguan versions) and against Manchu; the authors treat Jurchen as the ancestor of Manchu (p.10 'Nüzhen yu ji Manyu de zuyu'). No dialect is singled out; the reduction statement on p.178 is drawn from the Yongle Nüzhen yiyu transcriptions.

sources.citation: Joseph, Andrew J. 2018. The historical phonology of Manchu dialects. PhD dissertation, Cornell University.
sources.note: Treats Late Jurchen as a Manchu variety (sec.2.2.4, segmental inventory after Kane 1989); states (pp.60-61) that the Manchu accentual system is too poorly described for comparative reconstruction; no Jurchen stress statement.
